query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a coherent interfacial layer that forms an ordered L12-like phase in HEA multilayers will serve as a material bridge to transition the creep mechanism from being dominated by diffusion processes at high temperatures to dislocation-based deformation at lower temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A HEA multilayer coating with as-deposited, possibly partially incoherent interfaces.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a thin, engineered interfacial layer (using an L12-phase forming eutectic HEA such as an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 composition) that promotes a high degree of interface coherency with adjacent layers.
generation.conditions: Under creep testing over a range of elevated temperatures, where diffusion-mediated creep is more dominant at higher temperatures and dislocation-mediated creep becomes more significant as temperature decreases.
generation.structural_mediator: The coherent, ordered (L12-like) phase at the interface that minimizes lattice mismatch and acts as a barrier to homogeneous diffusion paths.
generation.mechanism: The coherent interlayer stabilizes the interface and reduces stress concentration by inhibiting rapid vacancy diffusion. At high temperatures, where atomic diffusion is active, this layer controls the creep rate by impeding diffusive flow. As temperature decreases, the preserved coherency facilitates the nucleation and motion of dislocations, thereby promoting dislocation-mediated creep.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEA multilayers with the engineered coherent interlayer are expected to exhibit a measurable shift in the creep mechanism transition temperature, displaying lower creep rates due to a controlled switch in deformation modes (from diffusion creep toward dislocation creep). The transition point is anticipated to shift relative to unmodified multilayers, though the exact magnitude of the effect remains to be quantified.
generation.baseline: Standard HEA multilayers without the engineered coherent L12 interlayer, where creep behavior is predominantly controlled by diffusion mechanisms at high temperatures and less clearly transitions to dislocation-based creep.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect should be observable only when the interfacial coherency is maintained; if the layer’s thickness, composition, or processing leads to excessive misfit or incoherency, the desired transition effect may not occur.
generation.uncertainty: The exact shift in transition temperature and the quantitative effects on overall creep rates are not yet determined and require experimental validation, given the limited direct studies on interface engineering in HEA multilayers.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of HEA multilayer samples: one set with the engineered, coherent interfacial layer derived from an L12-phase forming composition (e.g., an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic variant) and one set without such an interlayer. Subject both sets to creep tests over a broad temperature range. Use high-resolution microscopy (TEM and SEM) and diffraction techniques to verify interface coherency and examine microstructural changes over time.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves at multiple temperatures
Activation energy for creep measured from temperature-dependent creep tests
Dislocation density and motion via TEM
Interface structure and phase identification via XRD and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA multilayers with the engineered interfacial layer do not show a statistically significant shift in creep mechanism (evidenced by similar activation energies, similar dislocation activities, and no clear difference in strain rate behavior) compared to the unmodified samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
